summary:
Canopy: go when the park is at its best.

We built Canopy, a web app that shows the best month to visit each of the 63 US national parks. Visitors pick what they want, such as mild days, stargazing, waterfalls or fall colours. They can also pick what to avoid, such as heat, bugs, smoke or crowds. Canopy scores every park and month using NASA data: NASA POWER climate records, NASA FIRMS fire detections, and VIIRS night lights. Each park shows three views: 2026 so far, a 2027 trend, and a 2050 climate model from WorldClim CMIP6.

Canopy turns a raw NASA climate archive into one simple answer: when to go. It also shows how each park is changing. Statistical tests flag where warming is real and where it is just noise. Students learn this through park mysteries, and researchers get a full trend atlas.

This matters because a trip often happens once. A visit at the wrong time can mean extreme heat, smoke or closed trails. Climate change is moving those best weeks. Canopy helps people plan with real data and see the change for themselves.
details:
What it does

Canopy answers one question for any US national park: when should I go?

  1. Plan: The visitor picks months, how warm they like it, and what they're into. Choices include stargazing, waterfalls, wildflowers, fall colours, camping and long hikes. They can also pick what to avoid, such as heat, bugs, freezing nights, rain, smoke, fire season or crowds. Any choice can be a "must" or a "nice to have".
  2. Score: For every park and every month, the backend turns NASA climate data into a 0–100 match score. It shows the top parks, why #1 won, the best dates, and a year-round view of each park.
  3. Three horizons: Each park has three columns: 2026 so far (measured), 2027 trend (projected from the long-term trend) and 2050 model (CMIP6 climate projections). A "Go before it changes" list flags parks whose best months are getting worse.
  4. Save: Saved parks appear as postcards with the photo, the scores and the weather for all three horizons.
  5. Learn: Students solve park mysteries built on real data and collect passport stamps. Researchers can turn on a set of tools: a trend atlas, a topo map, analog sites, park families, season shifts, a robustness check, and park-versus-park comparisons.

How it works

  • Data-prep scripts download and process each dataset once, then save small JSON files in the repo. So the live app needs no API keys and loads fast.
  • For each park and month, the trend test uses Sen's slope (the median rate of change) and the Mann-Kendall test. A Benjamini-Hochberg correction then checks the results across all parks together. This way, "this park is warming" means a real signal, not noise.
  • Each filter becomes a 0–1 score from the data: snowmelt timing for waterfalls, cloud plus darkness plus night lights for stargazing, dew point for muggy air, and so on. The scores are weighted into one match score. A "must" that fails removes the park and tells you which single change would bring it back.

Benefits and intended impact

  • For visitors: a trip is often once in a lifetime. Canopy helps avoid smoke, extreme heat or snowed-in trails, and picks the month the park is at its best.
  • For students: climate change becomes something they can see in a park they know, through mysteries instead of lectures.
  • For researchers: park-level trends with honest statistics, which they can cite and compare.
  • The bigger goal: to show that climate change is already moving the best weeks to visit, using NASA data anyone can read.

Tools and languages

  • Backend: Python 3.13, FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, statsmodels, pymannkendall, rasterio. Data prep also used pandas, xarray, GeoPandas, Shapely and Google Earth Engine.
  • Frontend: TypeScript, React, Vite, Recharts, hand-drawn SVG maps.
  • Quality: pytest, Vitest, Testing Library, Ruff, ESLint, and GitHub Actions running the tests on every push.
  • Deploy: Docker, hosted on Render's free plan.
  • Hardware: ordinary laptops only. No special hardware.

What makes it creative

  • It turns a climate archive into a travel planner people actually want to use.
  • One page gives the past, the near future and 2050 side by side.
  • It mixes in games: park mysteries, passport stamps, "Guess the Twin" and a "since you were born" view.
  • Postcards and shareable trip cards make the data easy to share.

What the team considered

  • Honesty: guesses such as bugs, wildflowers and fall colours are marked as estimates. Every number names its source. The trend tests are corrected for testing many parks at once.
  • Plain words first: the default view uses everyday language. Scores, slopes and p-values appear only when research tools are on.
  • Edge cases:
    • Sequoia and Kings Canyon share one NPS code, so we split them.
    • American Samoa is south of the equator, so its seasons are flipped.
    • Parks with no snowpack get no waterfall score from snowmelt.
  • Access:
    • It works on phones.
    • Keyboard navigation works.
    • Motion is reduced for users who ask for it.
    • Every page has its own link.
  • Privacy and cost:
    • Accounts stay in the user's browser, with hashed passwords.
    • The app needs no paid APIs and runs on free hosting.
  • Licensing: every photo is free to use and credited.
